184804293.title: File:Fonio panicles maturing in Natitingou, northern Benin.jpg

ImageDescription.value:
Often called one of the world’s oldest cultivated cereals, fonio ('Digitaria exilis') produces these slender, seed-laden heads just before harvest. Though tiny and labor-intensive to process, the grains carry deep cultural roots and growing promise for nutrition and climate resilience.
Photo: Michael Major for Crop Trust

"Village chief of Boula Téné, [Senegal] Theodore Mada Keita, holds up the fonio grain [White fonio (Digitaria exilis)] that helps feed his family in southern Senegal. With USAID support, his community is working to better process and sell this nutritious grain, which is increasingly in demand in specialty markets overseas."  Original USAID caption. According to original article, Boula Tene is a Bedik village of 200 in the southeast of Senegal, Tambacounda region (since 2008: Kédougou Region).

184806441.title: File:Threshing fonio with a small-scale machine, Natitingou, northern Benin.jpg

ImageDescription.value:
After harvest, bundles of fonio ('Digitaria exilis') are fed into a locally adapted threshing machine to separate grain from straw. Mechanization at this stage can significantly reduce labour and post-harvest losses. For smallholders, access to shared equipment like this can make the difference between fonio as a subsistence crop and a viable source of income.

Farmer Ferdinand COMBETTI.

Photo: Michael Major for Crop Trust

184805184.title: File:Traditional fonio harvest with a sickle, Natitingou, northern Benin.jpg

ImageDescription.value:
Fonio ('Digitaria exilis') is still cut by hand in small bundles, the curved blade slicing through the slender stems close to the ground. The grain is tiny and the work meticulous. Harvesting and processing remain labour-intensive, carried out largely by smallholders using simple tools passed down through generations.

Fonio harvest at the farm of Mathias N’tcha-N’tcha, a retired pastor who planted his first crop of fonio based on recollections of his father.

Photo: Michael Major for Crop Trust
